papers.title: Dendrite Control Theory: A Unifying Framework Bridging Neuronal Morphology And Dendritic Voltage Behavior
papers.abstract: Control theory and dendritic computation have revolutionized their respective fields, yet they rarely converge. Here, we use control theory as a framework to reveal how dendritic morphology and synaptic input organization constrain structural resilience and energy cost. Treating diverse dendritic trees as connected network nodes, we demonstrate that the degree of structural symmetry dictates easy- versus hard-to-access control states. Notably, control inputs restricted solely to peripheral terminal branches are mathematically sufficient to govern the voltage states of the entire dendrite and soma, granting striking resilience against input loss elsewhere. Conversely, limiting input dimensionality amplifies voltage fluctuations and metabolic costs. These findings expose fundamental biophysical trade-offs between wiring cost, functional flexibility, robustness, and energy efficiency, suggesting interneurons generally exhibit higher resilience while excitatory neurons feature superior controllability. We introduce 'Dendrite Control Theory' as a rigorous engineering framework linking neuronal morphology directly to computation and robustness, offering a new neuroscience research paradigm.

papers.title: Asymmetric detection of relative speed during motion-based figure-ground segregation
papers.abstract: Visual motion can support figure-ground segregation when a local region moves at a different speed from its background, but whether faster- and slower-than-background targets are detected equally well, and how any asymmetry depends on background speed and motion reliability remains incompletely understood. We measured relative-speed detection thresholds in four human observers using an eight-alternative forced-choice localization task. On each trial, one of eight random-dot patches at 10-degree eccentricity moved either faster or slower than a surrounding moving background. Relative-speed detection thresholds were measured with adaptive staircases at five background speeds (2.5-30 deg/s) under 100% and 60% motion coherence. In every observer, slower targets required larger relative-speed differences for detection than faster targets. This increment-decrement asymmetry was strongest at low background speeds and diminished as speed increased. Reducing motion coherence elevated thresholds overall but disproportionately impaired detection of slower targets, amplifying the asymmetry, most strongly at the lowest measurable speeds. Under 100% coherence, increment detection showed approximately Weber-like scaling from 10 to 30 deg/s, whereas under reduced coherence both increment and decrement Weber fractions decreased with increasing background speed. Relative-speed detection therefore depends on the sign of the speed difference, background speed, and motion reliability. The faster-target advantage is consistent with faster-speed weighting reported in cortical area MT and with natural-scene statistics showing that figural regions tend to move faster than their backgrounds, suggesting that relative-speed sensitivity may contribute to motion-based figure-ground segregation. More broadly, such increment-decrement asymmetries can reveal biases in how sensory signals are represented and read out.

papers.title: Evaluating State-Transition Models in Short Resting-State fMRI with Continuous-Dynamics Controls
papers.abstract: Hidden Markov models (HMMs) are widely used to describe changes in resting-state functional MRI as transitions between a finite set of inferred brain states. However, continuously varying brain activity can produce similar apparent transitions, raising questions about their biological validity. We tested whether discrete and continuous brain dynamics could be distinguished by predicting subsequent fMRI measurements, and if temporal filtering affects this distinction. We compared hidden Markov models (HMMs) with vector autoregressive (VAR) models, which predict signals from preceding measurements without assuming discrete states. Each time point contained signals from the seven Yeo functional networks. Both models used the same preceding observations to predict the next, with accuracy measured by the log probability density assigned to the observed signals. Across 864 simulated conditions, HMMs performed better in 139/144 unfiltered discrete-state cases, whereas VAR performed better in 67/72 continuous cases. Changing only the filter during testing increased the number of continuous cases favoring HMMs from 2/72 with fixed filtering to 68/72, despite unchanged underlying dynamics. We also analyzed resting-state fMRI from 270 ADNI participants (90 cognitively normal, 90 with mild cognitive impairment, and 90 with dementia). VAR outperformed HMM in 160/184 datasets with at least 180 time points and 60/86 shorter recordings. In simulations, HMMs inferred directional state transitions even from smoothly evolving activity without discrete switching. Thus, apparent fMRI state transitions do not necessarily indicate discrete underlying dynamics. Their interpretation requires comparison with continuous models and attention to temporal filtering.

papers.title: Feedback Valence, Prediction Error, and the Limits of Computational Attribution in Symptom-Related EEG
papers.abstract: Feedback-locked electroencephalography (EEG) responses are often interpreted using model-derived prediction errors (PEs), although signed PE can be strongly coupled to feedback valence in binary-outcome tasks. We revisited a published anxiety-related EEG association using two open probabilistic-learning datasets to examine measurement reliability, predictor separability, and participant-level recovery. In the primary dataset, greater trait anxiety was associated with a larger negative-minus-positive FCz theta response among 46 participants with elevated depressive symptoms after adjustment for depression severity. The association also differed between the sampled depression-symptom groups. The feedback contrast showed useful within-session reliability, but matched delta and P3-minus-N2 analyses did not establish theta specificity. Within participants, feedback valence and signed PE were highly correlated (r = -0.964). Exact-design simulations showed that population-level model discrimination could succeed despite poor recovery of individual neural slopes. Participant-specific learning-model refits recovered overall signed PE more consistently than the within-valence variation needed to distinguish it from feedback valence. An independent dataset reproduced the FCz feedback contrast in untreated and placebo cohorts but lacked trait-anxiety scores. Adding signed PE to valence yielded a small held-out predictive improvement under one reinforcement-learning specification, with limited support across sessions and no comparable support under the dual-rate model or in placebo. Together, these findings support a symptom-related feedback EEG association while constraining its theta-specific and participant-level computational interpretation.

papers.title: Early Increases in Hippocampal Synchrony Predict Chronic Epileptiform Burden in a Temporal Lobe Epilepsy Model
papers.abstract: Temporal lobe epilepsy (TLE), the most common focal epilepsy, is often drug-resistant and arises predominantly in the hippocampus. Disease severity is conventionally assessed by seizure frequency and duration, yet epileptiform activity outside discrete seizures may also track disease progression. Whether this activity reflects hippocampal network reorganization as part of epileptogenesis, and whether such reorganization predicts chronic severity, is unknown. Here, we combined longitudinal two-photon calcium imaging of hippocampal CA1 neurons with repeated 24-hour EEG recordings that quantified epileptiform burden in the same pilocarpine treated mice over 16 weeks. CA1 firing and synchrony rose acutely, subsided during a latent period, and increased again chronically, with synchronized firing organized into brief waves that propagated in a consistent direction. Epileptiform burden followed a similar temporal trajectory and increasingly contained electrographic seizures. CA1 synchrony correlated with epileptiform burden and stratified mice into groups with distinct neuronal and electrographic outcomes. CA1 synchrony measured within three weeks of pilocarpine induction predicted chronic epileptiform burden, identifying early hippocampal synchrony as a candidate imaging biomarker and pointing to an early window for intervention in TLE.

papers.title: ACTIVATION OF THE ARYL HYDROCARBON RECEPTOR REDUCES VISCERAL HYPERSENSITIVITY IN A MOUSE MODEL OF COLITIS IN REMISSION
papers.abstract: The aryl hydrocarbon receptor (AhR) is expressed on gut-projecting transient receptor potential vanilloid-1 (TRPV1)+ nociceptors, but whether it has a role in regulating abdominal pain remains to be determined. Approximately 50% of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) patients experience chronic abdominal pain, even when their inflammatory disease is in remission. Previous work has shown that tryptophan metabolism to indole derivatives is reduced in IBD patients. Since microbial tryptophan metabolites (indole derivatives) serve as ligands for AhR, we hypothesized that reduced AhR activation contributes to enhanced pain sensitivity. We used a post-colitis mouse model of visceral hypersensitivity to examine the role of AhR as a mediator of nociception. AhR activation using both natural and synthetic agonists reduced visceral hypersensitivity in both male and female post-colitis mice. Conversely, pharmacological inhibition of AhR blocked the antinociceptive effects of indoles. Mechanistically, AhR activation by indole-3-pyruvic acid (IPyA) increased the transcription of the inward rectifying potassium channel Kir2.2, in TRPV1+ neurons and markedly reduced neuronal activation within the dorsal horn of the spinal cord. Metagenomic analysis revealed sex differences in indole-producing bacteria, with control males exhibiting enriched abundance of Akkermansia muciniphila and Alistipes compared to post-colitis males and female controls. These findings demonstrate that oral IPyA supplementation in post-colitis mice attenuates visceral hypersensitivity in part through activation of nociceptor AhR, providing insights that support the therapeutic targeting of AhR to treat abdominal pain in IBD patients in remission.

papers.title: Parallel descending neurons differentially encode target and looming information in the hoverfly visual system
papers.abstract: Detecting small, fast-moving objects is crucial for behaviors such as pursuit, territorial defence, and predator avoidance. At long range, however, potential mates, rivals, and predators produce remarkably similar visual signals, potentially making them difficult to distinguish. Nevertheless, many flying insects, including the hoverfly Eristalis tenax, can respond rapidly and appropriately to these ambiguous visual cues, implying specialised neural pathways that extract behaviorally relevant information. Descending neurons link visual processing to motor output, thus transforming visual signals into behavioral actions. In E. tenax, both target selective descending neurons (TSDNs) and looming-sensitive descending neurons respond to small targets, yet their respective contributions to target processing remain unclear. Using electrophysiological recordings, we compared receptive field organization and sensitivity to target size and motion direction across these neuronal populations. Although TSDNs and looming-sensitive descending neurons differed systematically in their target coding, a subset of looming-sensitive descending neurons closely resembled TSDNs, sharing small receptive fields and sharp target tuning despite retaining sensitivity to looming stimuli. These findings reveal previously unrecognized diversity among descending neurons tuned to small targets and suggest that parallel descending pathways encode distinct information from similar visual cues. Such an organization may enable common visual inputs to support both target pursuit and the detection of approaching threats.

papers.title: Traveling waves in attention networks inherit the rhythms of sensory systems
papers.abstract: Attention emerges from coordinated activity across distributed brain regions, each with their own intrinsic rhythm: alpha (7-12Hz) in visual cortex and theta (3-7Hz) in auditory cortex. When attention is sustained on a visual location, alpha power increases over the corresponding ipsilateral hemisphere, a robust neurophysiological marker of sustained visuospatial attention named alpha lateralization. Hemispheric asymmetry during sustained attention was recently also reported for anterior-to-posterior alpha traveling waves -smooth phase shifts across the cortex. This finding suggests that traveling waves support top-down inter-areal communication within the attention network. Here we asked whether traveling waves indeed reflect top-down attention signals or are merely a byproduct of sustained visuospatial attention. We manipulated attention through different sensory modalities (auditory cueing and visual stimulation), thus engaging different sensory cortices, while maintaining the task as visual discrimination. Using electroencephalography, we tested the hypothesis that if traveling waves reflect attention signals within the network, their frequency should follow the intrinsic rhythm of the engaged sensory system: theta for auditory cueing and alpha for visual stimulation. If instead they are a byproduct of attention allocated to visual information, their frequency should remain in alpha. Our results support the former: auditory cueing led to lateralized theta traveling waves, while visual stimulation produced lateralized alpha traveling waves. Crucially, traveling-wave lateralization in both frequencies correlated with trial-by-trial alpha power lateralization. Together, attention signals appear to propagate as waves at the intrinsic rhythm of the engaged sensory system and locally modulate alpha power lateralization in task-relevant visual regions.

papers.title: A Kernel-Spectral Index for Single-Neuron Input-Output Complexity
papers.abstract: The computational capacity of individual neurons in the brain is a central problem in computational neuroscience and an increasingly relevant link between neuroscience and AI. Recent work fitting artificial neural networks to detailed cortical pyramidal neurons showed that reproducing their millisecond-precision input-output behavior can require temporal convolutional networks with five to eight layers, suggesting that cortical neurons may function as deep computational units inside brain circuits. Yet current quantitative studies of single-neuron complexity are largely surrogate-based; consequently, the obtained results are difficult to interpret, and the process often demands massive computational resources. We introduce the Spectral Complexity Index (SCI), a white-box measure that represents presynaptic histories with an explicit kernel geometry and quantifies how many ordered spectral modes are needed to explain somatic response energy. Across 35 biophysically detailed human and mouse cortical neuron models, SCI yields a statistically significant separation of the two species, strongly agrees with the DNN-based Functional Complexity Index on these cells (Spearman correlation: {rho}=0.797), and remains stable under sampling and kernel perturbations. Additionally, compared to existing methods such as FCI, the computational cost of SCI is reduced to approximately 1/10 or less. SCI turns single-neuron complexity from a black-box surrogate property into an interpretable spectral object, enabling reproducible, fast, and efficient comparisons of neuronal computation across cells and species.

papers.title: An open-access neuroimaging-compatible virtual town task for assessing human spatial navigation
papers.abstract: Spatial navigation is a cognitive skill that draws on multiple processes such as learning, decision-making and memory, which are often updated on a second-by-second timescale. However, many existing virtual paradigms designed to assay spatial navigation cannot target these processes as they unfold or are not designed for integration with concurrent neurophysiological recording. Here, we present and demonstrate our open-access task for neuroimaging: NAturalistic Virtual Assessment of Navigation (NAVAN) combining high-resolution behavioural tracking and integration with electroencephalography. We report data from this task, in which fifty-three participants completed a wayfinding navigation paradigm across twenty-four trials. Navigational efficiency improved significantly following repeated exposure to the environment, although efficiency declined across trials within each block. Self-reported spatial ability (assessed by the Santa Barbara Sense of Direction) predicted performance during early environmental exposure, suggesting concurrent validity. We demonstrated the feasibility of recording electroencephalography during the task, with in-game events streamed and aligned to the neural recording. The task provides researchers with access to detailed behavioural measures and can be adapted by modifying features such as trial number and difficulty. We also provide a step-by-step implementation guide to support reuse and customisation across experimental settings.

papers.title: Age-specific pediatric templates improve EEG source-reconstructed biomarkers in children
papers.abstract: EEG source reconstruction requires an anatomical head model, ideally constructed from individual magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scans. In developmental studies of children and adolescents, however, MRIs are rarely available. Researchers therefore routinely rely on adult templates, such as the FreeSurfer average (fsaverage), despite substantial anatomical changes throughout development. How much this reliance on adult models biases downstream EEG biomarkers remains unclear. Here, we investigated whether age-specific pediatric templates offer a better alternative to fsaverage for EEG-derived biomarkers in children and adolescents, using individual MRI-based reconstruction as the reference. We analyzed eyes-closed resting-state EEGs from 384 Healthy Brain Network participants aged 5.5 to 17.5 years. For each participant, we tested three anatomical models: their individual MRI, an age-specific pediatric template from a series spanning ages 6-17 at one-year intervals, and the adult fsaverage template. We compared four EEG biomarkers in childhood and adolescence: absolute power, relative power, long-range temporal correlations quantified with detrended fluctuation analysis (DFA), and functional excitation-inhibition (fE/I) ratio. Pediatric templates agreed more closely with individual MRI-based biomarkers in both developmental groups and had fewer parcels with significantly different biomarker values than the adult template, except for absolute power in older adolescents. We conclude that when individual MRI is not available, age-specific pediatric templates match individual MRI-based EEG biomarker values more closely than the adult template across all four biomarkers up to approximately 12 years of age and should be the preferred choice at least up to this age.

papers.title: Common attentional mechanisms, but distinct computational dynamics, across Statistical and Reward Learning
papers.abstract: Past experience guides attention through statistical learning (SL) and reward learning (RL). Yet, whether they do so through similar neural and computational mechanisms remains unclear. In a first EEG visual-search experiment, we tested whether RL establishes latent spatial representations, previously demonstrated for SL. Afterwards, we directly compared RL and SL in a double-session experiment. Using multivariate decoding, Experiment 1 showed that high-reward locations could be decoded before target onset following a task-irrelevant, spatially-unspecific visual perturbation. Experiment 2 revealed that SL and RL established comparable neural representations, and similarly facilitated target selection and evidence accumulation (drift-rate). However, combining Rescorla-Wagner and Drift Diffusion Model revealed slower learning-rate for RL than SL. Pupillometry further tracked spatially selective expectation violations during SL, but reflected increased arousal during RL. Together, our results reveal how the brain routes distinct computational algorithms (probability estimation versus value caching) into a unified attentional priority map.

papers.title: ClearGel: a thermoresponsive hydrogel for chronic, near-millimeter two-photon imaging through the intact skull
papers.abstract: The intact skull remains a fundamental barrier to high-resolution two-photon neuroimaging in live mice. Existing skull-clearing methods, however, cannot simultaneously provide deep cortical access, spatial selectivity, reversibility, and biological safety. Here we introduce ClearGel, a thermoresponsive hydrogel that undergoes rapid in situ gelation upon contact with the skull, confining the clearing agents to the targeted region while sustaining their release over time. ClearGel routinely enables two-photon imaging down to approximately 800 m through the intact skull-a depth statistically equivalent to open-skull windows and substantially surpassing all prior approaches. It supports user-defined clearing patterns from focal sites to whole-skull coverage, allows repeated imaging over 14 days through a reversible optical interface, and, critically, enables awake functional imaging of both neuronal Ca2+ activity and the more elusive cAMP dynamics at single-cell resolution. ClearGel requires only simple topical application-no craniotomy or skull thinning-and provides a minimally invasive, chronic-compatible optical window for longitudinal studies of cortical function in behaving mice.

papers.title: LCN2+ Astrocytes Mark a Pro-inflammatory Astrocyte State Associated with Secondary Brain Injury After Cerebral Venous Thrombosis
papers.abstract: Cerebral venous thrombosis (CVT) is a cerebrovascular disorder with unique pathophysiological characteristics. Although the mortality rate during the acute phase has declined in recent years, the cellular mechanisms underlying secondary brain injury and long-term neurological dysfunction after CVT remain poorly understood [1,2]. In this study, we performed single-cell RNA sequencing of brain tissues from a murine CVT model to systematically characterize the cellular landscape following CVT and identified a reactive astrocyte state characterized by high expression of Lcn2. This astrocyte subset was markedly enriched after CVT. Notably, despite the absence of significant changes in the overall proportion of astrocytes, this population exhibited enhanced inflammatory/cytokine response signatures, ferroptosis-related stress responses, and vascular-immune microenvironment remodeling programs, suggesting that the major alteration of astrocytes after CVT is driven primarily by state transition rather than cellular expansion. Pseudotime trajectory analysis further demonstrated that Lcn2+ astrocytes were predominantly localized at the late stage of the trajectory and displayed sustained upregulation of multiple inflammation- and stress-associated genes, supporting their characterization as a late-stage reactive astrocyte state under CVT conditions. Cell-cell communication analysis revealed extensive predicted interactions between this subset and myeloid cells, vascular-associated cells, as well as neuronal/synaptic populations, indicating its potential involvement in dynamic remodeling of the lesion microenvironment. Cross-model integration analysis further revealed the presence of Lcn2-high astrocytes in the middle cerebral artery occlusion (MCAO) model; however, their expression breadth and intensity were generally weaker than those observed in CVT, suggesting that this cellular state may represent a common reactive framework following cerebrovascular obstruction, while being particularly pronounced in CVT. Furthermore, genetic deletion of LCN2 alleviated CVT-induced brain tissue injury in vivo, providing functional evidence supporting the detrimental role of the LCN2-associated pathological state. Collectively, our study identifies a distinct Lcn2-high reactive astrocyte state after CVT that is closely associated with inflammatory amplification, ferroptosis-related stress, and microenvironmental remodeling. These findings provide new cellular insights into the mechanisms underlying secondary brain injury after CVT and highlight potential targets for therapeutic intervention.

papers.title: Increased activity without changes in coupling between somata and apical dendrites during visual mismatches
papers.abstract: Leading theories of cortical function posit that sensory processing involves a comparison between top-down predictions and bottom-up sensory data. Tests of these theories have been hampered by experimental challenges related to simultaneously recording top-down and bottom-up signals in response to sensory stimuli that either do or do not match internally-generated predictions. Here, we conduct dual-plane 2-photon calcium imaging near-simultaneously from distal apical dendrites and somata of pyramidal neurons in each of 4 different regions of mouse visual cortex while the mice are presented with visual sequences that can either match or mismatch previously habituated visual stimuli. Specifically, we examine the responses in the distal apical dendrites and cell bodies of pyramidal neurons while mice view either movie clips that reverse unexpectedly or Gabor patch sequences that have orientations that do not match habituated patterns. We find that in response to unexpected reversals in natural movies, both the apical dendrites and somata show increased activity that decreases over repeated exposures, consistent with a prediction error response. However, we do not find any clear evidence for increased activity in response to mismatches in Gabor sequences, beyond possible release from adaptation effects. We additionally use volumetric images to connect dendritic and somatic compartments and examine the coupling between connected dendrites and cell bodies in layer 5 pyramidal neurons. We do not find evidence for changes in coupling in response to mismatch stimuli, either for natural movies or Gabor sequences. Our results are consistent across four regions of visual cortex. We also observe that increased responses to reversals in natural movies are stronger in layer 2/3 than layer 5 pyramidal neurons. Altogether, these data suggest that visual cortex is sensitive to deviations from previously-experienced naturalistic inputs. Our data do not suggest that this mismatch sensitivity extends to artificial stimuli, nor do they support theories of prediction error causing changes in the coupling between apical dendrites and somata.

papers.title: Social vision expands into auditory cortices of people born deaf: evidence from naturalistic film and encoding models
papers.abstract: Comparing deaf and hearing adults provides insight into the contribution of experience to function of auditory cortical networks. We used naturalistic fMRI and voxel-wise encoding to measure information processing in auditory networks of deaf (n=24) and hearing (n=22) adults who watched a 35-minute silent animated film. Unlike simpler stimuli, naturalistic films are rich in a broad range of perceptual, affective, and social features, including motion, dynamic social interactions, and Theory of Mind. Machine vision algorithms and human coding were used to densely annotate visual and social film features. In both groups we observed a right-lateralized processing hierarchy with encoding of low-level visual features in early visual areas, social visual features along the superior temporal sulcus (STS) and Theory of Mind in temporoparietal junction. In deaf participants, auditory cortices showed enhanced encoding of a broad range of visual information, from low level motion to Theory of Mind. In higher order auditory networks, social interactions emerging as the strongest predictor of neural activity in deaf people and showed the strongest enhancement in deafness. Auditory networks of deaf adults showed systematic anatomical organization within and across hemispheres. Within the right hemisphere, higher-order auditory regions neighboring the STS preferentially responded to social visual features whereas lower-level visual features were represented broadly across the auditory hierarchy. These results suggest that proximity and connectivity principles govern anatomical expansion of information encoding in sensory loss.

papers.title: 40 Hz visual stimulation increases gamma-band functional connectivity between visual, parietal and frontal regions
papers.abstract: Visual stimulation at 40 Hz is being investigated as a non-invasive intervention for Alzheimer's disease. Its neural responses have been reported in regions beyond the visual cortex, and concurrent cognitive tasks have been shown to increase their spatial extent. However, it is unclear whether these responses reflect increased functional connectivity between regions or a common response to the stimulus, and whether a concurrent task changes this connectivity. We recorded EEG from 29 healthy young adults during Regular 40 Hz flicker and Irregular 30-50 Hz flicker, each with and without a target-counting task (2 x 2 within-participant design). Source-space connectivity between visual, parietal, and frontal regions was estimated with the debiased squared weighted phase-lag index (dWPLI). Regular stimulation increased 38-42 Hz connectivity for all three region pairs, with the largest increase between visual and parietal regions (increase in all 29 participants). The increase was specific to the stimulation frequency and was observed with two source reconstruction methods and in sensor space. The visual-parietal increase remained significant after correction for source leakage (spatial mixing between reconstructed sources) and after removal of the estimated stimulus-locked component, whereas the increases in visual-frontal and parietal-frontal connectivity did not. The concurrent task did not modulate the visual-parietal effect. For visual-frontal and parietal-frontal connectivity, the stimulation-by-ask interaction was not significant. These results show that 40 Hz visual stimulation increases gamma-band connectivity beyond the visual cortex, and much of this increase reflects a common stimulus-locked response, and connectivity beyond this response was observed mainly between visual and parietal regions.

papers.title: The C. elegans Connectome Toolbox: an open, extensible framework for multimodal connectomic data integration and analysis
papers.abstract: The nematode C. elegans is one of the best studied model organisms in biology. Since the initial description of the C. elegans neuronal connectome by White and colleagues, numerous studies have mapped and analyzed the connectome, and released structured datasets of the connectivity, often merging and adding to previous versions. These datasets now serve as foundational resources that underpin studies into the neuronal basis of C. elegans behavior. In spite of their high utility, heterogeneity in the different datasets and their annotation conventions obscures direct comparison where discrepancies between connectomes frequently stem from differences in coverage or nomenclature rather than genuine biological disagreement. Additionally, datasets describing new connectivity modalities - contact-based (the contactome), extrasynaptic (monoaminergic and neuropeptidergic), and functional connectivity - have also recently become available. Thus, there is a need for a unified framework providing standardized access to these diverse datasets while preserving their individual provenance. Here, we present the C. elegans Connectome Toolbox, a comprehensive framework for consolidating, curating and validating historical and newly published multimodal C. elegans connectivity data. Connectome Toolbox includes an accessible online resource (https://openworm.org/ConnectomeToolbox) for interactive data exploration and is accompanied by a Python library for programmatic access. We demonstrate the utility of the toolbox through a series of analyses that illustrate how connectome data can be explored, visualized, and compared across modalities, including integration of the anatomical connectome with a comprehensive neurotransmitter atlas, and comparison with computational models of C. elegans neural circuits.

papers.title: Temporal stability for individual differences in both habit learning and expression
papers.abstract: Actions transition from goal-directed to stimulus-driven habits through repetition. Individual differences in the capacity to learn and control habits are central to current models of psychopathology, which assume that overreliance on habitual control drives maladaptive behaviors. However, whether these tendencies reflect stable, trait-like cognitive processes remains unclear. We examined the temporal stability of individual differences in habit learning and expression. Across two preregistered experiments (total N = 313), we assessed stimulus-response habits using the same stimuli after one day or different stimuli after four months. Evidence for stable individual differences in habit commissions was strong and comparable across experiments, with computational modelling further supporting trait-like tendencies for habit learning and expression. Trait-like tendencies were also reflected in action automatization while practicing stimulus-response associations, which was associated with future habitual behavior. Our findings have theoretical implications for our understanding of habit formation and its role in psychopathology.

papers.title: Sex differences in cell type-specific transcriptional programs and GPCR signaling in the human subgenual anterior cingulate cortex
papers.abstract: Psychiatric conditions show marked sex differences in disease onset, symptom presentation, and response to treatments. Understanding how sex differences manifest across molecularly distinct neuronal populations in individuals without psychiatric conditions may help explain sex-dependent variation in neural circuit function and treatment response. Here, we examined molecularly distinct cell types within the subgenual anterior cingulate cortex (sgACC) of non-psychiatric subjects. Using RNA sequencing data previously generated from laser-capture microdissected neurons, we investigated sex differences in gene expression and co-expression networks in excitatory pyramidal neurons (layers 2/3 and 5/6) and somatostatin (SST)-, parvalbumin (PVALB)-, and vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP)-expressing inhibitory interneurons (N=10 males, 9 females). We identified sex differences in transcriptomic profiles, biological pathways, and co-expression network connectivity. PVALB cells showed stronger overall female transcriptional enrichment, while SST cells exhibited male-enriched transcriptional signatures. Weighted gene co-expression network analysis identified PVALB and SST modules more connected in males and females, respectively, which included hub genes involved in immune, extracellular matrix, and bioenergetic processes. Since G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) are viable therapeutic targets, we examined sex differences in GPCR transcripts. Across all GPCR-cell-type combinations, CHRM2 in PVALB cells showed the second strongest sex difference (enriched in females). To test the functional relevance of this difference, we used patch-clamp electrophysiology in mouse prefrontal cortex. M2 receptor activation increased maximal firing rates in PVALB cells from female but not male mice. Collectively, our findings demonstrate cell type-specific sex differences in the sgACC corresponding to functional differences in neuromodulator signaling, with potential implications for treatment response.

papers.title: A red fluorescent sensor for intensity-and lifetime imaging of cAMP in living cells
papers.abstract: cAMP (cyclic adenosine monophosphate) is a crucial intracellular messenger involved in neuromodulation and plasticity, but more information on its spatiotemporal regulation is desirable. Here we constructed a red fluorescent indicator based on a truncated cAMP binding site derived from a regulatory PKA subunit of protozoan origin. It contains a single binding site for cAMP highly specific for cAMP over cGMP. chILI (cAMP highly-responsive Intensity and Lifetime Indicator) can be imaged as an intensity-based probe, but alternatively also offers options for fluorescence lifetime imaging. When expressed in the mouse brain using AAV-vector mediated gene transfer, it reports spontaneous and evoked cAMP transients from CA1 neurons in the hippocampus of awake mice. chILI will add valuable options for monitoring cAMP in vitro and in vivo.

papers.title: Naturalistic recall preserves temporal specificity despite cortical feature reorganization
papers.abstract: Although sensory input arrives in a largely continuous stream, recall is temporally compressed, discontinuous, and often structured as events. However, the temporal specificity of recall-related neural activity within events, and the separation and cortical organization of recalled features relative to perception, remain poorly characterized. We analyzed functional MRI data recorded during viewing and free recall of an episode of Sherlock. A data-driven alignment between viewing and recall data identified neural recapitulation of corresponding narrative events and revealed information that distinguished moments within events, particularly in the association cortex. Features ranging from low-level visual to semantic information predicted recall reinstatement. However, differences in predictive performance among feature levels became smaller during recall, and their organization along the cortical sensory-to-association gradient reversed relative to viewing. Thus, temporal specificity within events can be preserved despite substantial reorganization of feature representations across the cortex during recall.

papers.title: Unilateral naris occlusion with custom-made plugs for reversible olfactory deprivation in juvenile and adult mice
papers.abstract: Deprivation paradigms that reduce environmental input have been successfully applied across multiple species and sensory modalities, including vision, audition, somatosensation, and olfaction in order to understand how neurons and circuits respond to loss of sensory input. One notable advantage of studying sensory deprivation in the rodent olfactory system is the ease and control with which smell loss can be induced. Various methods of olfactory deprivation have long been available and rely on blocking a nostril, either through invasive and often non-reversible approaches such as chemical ablation or surgical procedures, or through reversible approaches such as unilateral naris occlusion using custom-made nose plugs. Here, we provide a systematic description of this well-established method, including its construction from commercially available materials, procedures, validation, and reliability in post-weaning mice, thereby providing a detailed and reproducible framework for controlled, reversible olfactory deprivation.

papers.title: Locomotor activity enhances environmental representation by boosting visuo-frontal communication
papers.abstract: During environment exploration we rapidly acquire visual information to identify targets of interest. Here, we discovered that locomotion limits how long natural scenes are viewed dur- ing free exploration. Whether the brain has developed compensatory mechanisms to ensure that sensory information is accurately transmitted to downstream areas during and after locomotion is unknown. We examined this issue by recording the spiking activity of popula- tions of neurons in visual and prefrontal cortex in conjunction with wireless recordings of oculomotor events while macaques moved freely to explore their environment or performed treadmill bipedal locomotion. The communication between visuo-frontal cortical areas was enhanced during and after locomotion to increase visual-evoked responses and population coding accuracy in prefrontal, but not visual cortical neurons. This in turn improved behav- ioral performance in a freely moving visual detection task after locomotion. Electrical stim- ulation further revealed elevated inter-areal synaptic efficacy during locomotor activity. The mechanism whereby locomotion enhances stimulus coding accuracy in prefrontal cortex and behavioral performance by increasing visuo-frontal communication is functionally beneficial during environmental exploration when incoming stimuli are rapidly changing and the win- dow for perceptual decisions is temporally restricted.

papers.title: An Eyewear-Based EEG Interface for Temporal-Region Monitoring and Emotion Recognition
papers.abstract: Conventional electroencephalography (EEG) devices are often impractical for ambulatory settings due to their reliance on specialized hardware and expert operation. To address this, we developed a user-friendly eyewear-based EEG system featuring dry titanium electrodes positioned approximately 5 mm inferoposterior to the T7/T8 sites (near the ears), with metal nose pads serving as references. We evaluated the system across 103 recordings spanning five paradigms: alpha reactivity, blink-related transients, fatigue, attention, and video-elicited emotion. Following quality control, 93.2-100.0% of epochs were retained. The system demonstrated high sensitivity to ocular transients, showing significant amplitude increases during the blinking task. The emotion task yielded the most robust state-related features, with statistically significant differences in differential entropy across negative, neutral, and positive video categories, achieving balanced accuracies of 0.882 for two-class and 0.667 for three-class prediction. Despite challenges at the multiple testing correction stage, the alpha reactivity and fatigue contrast tasks were still noteworthy to some extent. The attention paradigm revealed a consistent increase in differential entropy during focused states, and the eyewear system outperformed the Muse headband in group-held-out classification. These findings provide strong evidence for the feasibility of temporal-region eyewear EEG acquisition, highlighting its potential applications in the real-world, particularly for emotion recognition.

papers.title: Monoaminergic changes are associated with impaired neurogenesis along the longitudinal axis of the hippocampus in ageing and dementia
papers.abstract: Neurogenesis persists in the adult human hippocampus and is thought to support memory and emotional regulation. Both normal ageing and Parkinson disease dementia (PDD) are associated with reduced hippocampal neurogenesis, but why this occurs and how this might change across the across the hippocampal axis remains unclear. Here, we quantified the expression of genes regulating neurogenesis from stem cell production to neuron maturation and examined their relationship with monoaminergic activity throughout the post-mortem hippocampus in young and aged individuals, as well as in individuals with PDD. DCX and MKI67 expression were markedly reduced in PDD cases throughout the hippocampus, while GFAP and GFAP{delta} were elevated in aged control individuals but not in PDD. Dopamine and serotonin levels were unchanged but reduced levels of the dopamine metabolite DOPAC, and increased levels of the serotonin metabolite 5-HIAA, were present across the hippocampal axis in PDD. Hierarchical regression analysis identified DOPAC and 5-HIAA as significant predictors of DCX and MKI67 expression independent of diagnostic group. Coupling between stem cell markers and proliferative output was preserved in the hippocampus of young controls but was absent in aged controls and in PDD. These data suggest changes in monoaminergic systems are linked to stage-specific deficits in neuronal proliferation and maturation, identifying a potential mechanistic bridge to cognitive decline in PDD.

papers.title: Inosine Triphosphate Pyrophosphatase as a Candidate Associated with White Matter Abnormalities in Chronic Heart Failure
papers.abstract: Background: White matter hyperintensities (WMHs) are common with normal brain aging and frequently observed also in chronic heart failure (CHF). However, the relationship between CHF and white matter abnormalities and the biological factors remain unclear. We investigated WMH and associated white matter microstructural changes, such as fractional anisotropy (FA), in CHF and explored candidate molecular factors. Methods: We conducted a longitudinal prospective observation including brain T2-FLAIR magnetic resonace imaging for 32 asymptomatic Stage B (mean age 63.3{+/-}10.5 years; 25% women) and 23 symptomatic Stage C CHF patients (mean age 67.3{+/-}7.1 years; 30% women). Plasma proteomics and Mendelian randomization (MR) were used to identify candidate proteins associated with both CHF and WMH. The association of candidate proteins was further investigated using complementary analyses in CHF rats, cultured cortical neurons, and community-based genetic data in UK Biobank. Results: Global WMH volume increased more in Stage C than Stage B patients, predominantly near the anterior periventricular white matter, despite comparable cardiac indices (4,717{+/-}5,335 mm3 vs. 2,116{+/-}3,134 mm3, P=0.027). SomaScan-based proteomic analysis of plasma samples from this patient cohort revealed that 44 proteins are significantly associated with both Stage C CHF and WMH progression (P<0.05). Of these 44 proteins, two-step Mendelian randomization analysis identified inosine triphosphate pyrophosphatase (ITPA) as the only candidate protein, further supported by an association between rare variants in ITPA and FA. In CHF rats, the anterior pericallosal cortex showed decreases in myelin basic protein density and FA and an increase in ITPA expression compared to sham rats. In cultured cortical neurons, recombinant ITPA exposure reduced total axonal length. Conclusions: Symptomatic CHF was associated with WMH and impaired white matter integrity. ITPA emerged as a candidate factor across human, animal, and cellular analyses. These findings provide a basis for investgating the biological pathways linking CHF and white matter injury.

papers.title: Disentangling visual and motor contributions to continuous psychophysics
papers.abstract: Continuous psychophysics measures visual function by asking observers to track a randomly moving target. Because continuous responses provide more information than traditional discrete judgements, a few minutes of tracking can estimate visual sensitivity, making the approach attractive for testing children and patients. Tracking performance is often summarized by cross-correlating the target and cursor velocities: the resulting cross-correlogram peak, lag and width index how strongly, quickly and sharply the observer responds to the target. Tracking, however, requires both seeing the target and moving the cursor towards it, so poor tracking may reflect impaired vision, impaired motor control, or both. Here, we test whether visual and motor contributions to tracking performance can be told apart. Participants tracked a target with a computer mouse while wearing glasses that simulate two levels of visual impairment, using either their dominant or their non-dominant hand. We find that both manipulations alter the cross-correlogram metrics, lowering the peak correlation and delaying and broadening the response, but in different proportions. Visual impairment mainly delays and broadens the response, and does so in proportion to each participant's loss of visual acuity. The non-dominant hand mainly lowers the peak correlation. Two signatures of motor control explain this difference: with the non-dominant hand, participants pause more often and for longer, and move more noisily between pauses, whereas visual impairment alters neither. Together, response lag, time paused and movement noise reveal whether a change in tracking is visual or motor in almost every participant. Our findings demonstrate that, given a baseline measurement, the same tracking data that measure vision can also reveal whether a change in performance reflects a change in what an individual sees or in how they move.

papers.title: Loneliness as a modulator of intersubject neural alignment across social and nonsocial contexts
papers.abstract: Loneliness is associated with cognitive biases that diverge from normative patterns of understanding and may be reflected in altered neural responses to the world. Here, we examined how loneliness modulates neural synchrony across individuals during the processing of social and nonsocial information. Using high-resolution movie-watching fMRI data (n = 178) from the Human Connectome Project, we applied intersubject correlation analyses to identify context-dependent neural signature of loneliness. Lonely individuals primarily showed more idiosyncratic responses in regions within the default mode network, visual association cortex, and amygdala during social contexts, and in reward-related circuitry during nonsocial contexts. This suggests less stereotyped processing of social information and reward in lonely individuals. In contrast, lonely individuals exhibited greater neural synchrony in the nucleus accumbens during social contexts and in somatomotor regions during nonsocial contexts. This potentially reflects shared experiences of social craving and engagement with a socially irrelevant physical environment. These effects were robust against demographic similarities, kinship, depression, and objective levels of social connection. Together, these findings identify loneliness as a modulator of intersubject neural alignment, which may contribute to shaping how individuals process and interpret different aspects of the world.

papers.title: Disrupted mannosidase enzymes in C9orf72 ALS/FTD
papers.abstract: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is an age-related neurodegenerative disorder resulting from the loss of motor neurons in the brain and spinal cord. Neuroinflammation, induced by glial cells including microglia (MG) and astrocytes, is an acknowledged aspect of this neurodegeneration. Generating induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC) neuroinflammatory models of ALS may help elucidate non-neuronal mechanisms of disease. Here, we analyze human postmortem tissue and an iPSC derived glia-crosstalk model identifying a reduction in Golgi enzymes MAN1A1 and MAN1A2 in addition to other glycan enzymes from ALS-associated microglia and astrocytes. Impaired Golgi and glycan metabolism is linked to inflammation and other related ALS disease mechanisms including impaired lysosomal proteostasis, altered extracellular matrix, disrupted secretion, and altered cell-cell signaling.
